newsitem.title: USA: Faster, larger US tax refunds may lift Q1 spending.
newsitem.headline: Faster, larger US tax refunds may lift Q1 spending.

text.p: The Internal Revenue Service usually gets a bad rap. But this year, U.S. consumers might cheer the IRS for sending federal income tax refund checks out faster than any year this decade.
Refunds are already running about 20 percent ahead of last year's pace and are on course to total billions more than in 1996, a feature of an economy with higher job growth and income growth.

"This may be a temporary phenomenon, but there is so much more money sloshing around," said William Sullivan, director of money market research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "The numbers are so huge it could provide support for spending and may give the economy an added lift in the first quarter."
In recent years, the pattern of refund mailings has changed, affecting consumer spending patterns, economists said.

"Two years ago, the IRS dragged its feet and it showed up in retail sales (figures). February (1995) was weak, but when we got out to April and May it got stronger," noted Jim Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.
Statisticians at the Commerce Department said that if consumers spend their refunds this year, it may boost the February retail sales numbers, since seasonal factors won't pick it up.

Economists are currently forecasting around a 0.5 percent rise to February retail sales and a 0.4 percent increase in sales excluding autos. February retail sales will be released on Thursday, March 13.
Through the first three weeks of February 1997, the IRS has sent out more than $16 billion in refunds, well above the $9.5 billion in February 1996, according to the Treasury department.
"No doubt this is a lot of cash, and the reality is that there are billions (of dollars) more into households' pocketbooks this February than any other February," said Dean Witter's Sullivan.

In addition, the average size of refunds has jumped to $1,565 after the first three mailings this season, from $1,418 the same period last year. And that is with 0.6 percent fewer tax returns processed, the IRS said.
Don Roberts, an IRS spokesman, said it is doubtful this year's average refund will be that large.

The 1995 filing year garnered a $1,244 average refund, up 5.6 percent from $1,178 in 1994. The size of the average refund for the 1996 filing year should be five to seven percent above last year's level, he said.
Some economists argued that the higher average refund is due to consumers over-withholding on their 1996 taxes.

The quicker pace of refunds comes as electronic and phone filing are running well above last year's levels. Analysts noted that since many filers may opt for direct deposit of their refunds into bank accounts, rather than waiting for a check to arrive, consumers will receive refunds faster.

Thus, spending may be more evenly spread out instead of seeing a bump up in spending in May and June. Typically, the bulk of refunds are sent out in mid-April through June. "We're 19 percent ahead of last year (in dollar terms), which is significant," said Mitchell Held, chief economist at Smith Barney Inc. "There should be more spending near term and less in the second and third quarters. It is a factor that helps to explain some of the relative strength in the consumer this year."

Yet, Held and others said it is still difficult to quantify the effects of quicker refunds. Some analysts contend it has little or no impact since consumers use the money to pay down debts from the recent holiday season. And others said that Easter shopping adds a bigger chunk to spending data than do tax refunds.
"This is an open question. People are still debating it," said William Dudley, chief U.S. economist at Goldman Sachs & Co. "But it could make (spending data) stronger if they spend their (refunds)."

Indeed, retail sales jumped 2.1 percent in February 1996 year-over-year, which, some said reflected the faster pace of refunds last year over 1995. In 1995, February retail sales fell one percent, in a month where the refund pace was very slow.

"The data support more spending" from refunds, said Robert Brusca, chief economist at Nikko Securities Co. "By and large, people spend more than they pay down credit card debt. "They earned it so they say they can do something with it," he added. "People treat (refunds) as found money, and found money is spent."

Data released on Monday showed a slight drop in the amount of refunds in the February 28 mailing, at $5.4 billion, from the prior two mailings, which were both above $6 billion. Analysts said it could be that filers who knew they were getting big refunds filed as early as possible to get that refund quicker.
"It's a little early to draw any conclusions," said Glassman, cautioning that a stronger February might mean weaker spending in upcoming months. (( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
